content:
ComfyUIにネイティブMultiGPU機能がマージ！画像・動画生成が劇的に高速化！🚀

画像生成AIの最強ツール「ComfyUI」に、複数GPUをネイティブにサポートする新機能「CORE-184」がマージされました！これは複数GPU環境を持つクリエイターにとって、まさにゲームチェンジャーです！

💡 何がすごいの？
処理を「Work Units」に分割し、複数のGPUで同時に並行処理。具体的には「CFG並列化」を利用し、ポジティブとネガティブの計算を別々のGPUで同時に行います。

これにより、以下のような重い処理が劇的にスピードアップ！
・ポジティブ／ネガティブの両方を細かく指定した生成
・複数の「コンディショニング」（生成をコントロールする位置やマスクなどの指示情報）を使う複雑な生成
・「AnimateDiff-Evolved」などのフレーム数の多い動画生成

⚠️ 知っておくべきポイントと注意点
・既存のワークフローに「MultiGPU Work Units」ノードを追加するだけでOK！1つのGPUしかない環境でもノードが自動で無視されるため、ワークフローが壊れる心配はありません。
・ただし、負荷の軽い処理では、データの分割と合流にかかる「オーバーヘッド」のせいで、逆に遅くなる場合があります。重い処理でこそ真価を発揮する機能です！

💼 ビジネス・実務へのメリット
動画生成案件や、大量のプロトタイプを高速で出力したいスタジオにとって、レンダリング時間の短縮はそのまま「人件費の削減」と「納期短縮」に直結します。

自社でGPUを複数積んだマシンを運用している方や、クラウドGPUを活用している実践者の方は、ぜひこの新しいワークフローを導入して、競合に圧倒的な差をつけちゃいましょう！✨

title: From 15 hours to one minute: How AI/ML is speeding up GM's development
content: When we met Sterling Anderson in 2024 , he was the chief product officer of Aurora, the self-driving startup he cofounded in 2016 after several years at Tesla. Just over a year ago, though, Anderson decamped from the startup world for something a little more established, taking over as chief product officer at General Motors, the nation's largest automaker. Since then, he's had a good view of how GM is entering what he calls the third epoch of engineering and design. "There was a time when humans looked at birds and were like, 'OK, those wings seem to work pretty well. Let's go and design something that looks like them.'" Anderson said, describing the first age of engineering. "And they just kind of iterated their way to something that was marginally feasible." The first few hundred years of inventing "was this era of highly empirical iterative design development and engineering," he said. "And by that I mean humans largely started with what we know or had seen, built prototypes of something that kind of looked like it and maybe tweaked some things, hoping to make it perform better, tested it, iterated, and kind of went through this slow guess-and-check process until we got to something that marginally worked." title: China has approved the world’s first invasive brain-computer chip—here’s what’s next
content: One day last October, sitting in the courtyard of his house in China’s Henan province, Dong Hui decided to see if he could hold a pen to write.  Dong, 39, had sustained spinal cord injuries in a car accident six years earlier that left him paralyzed from the neck down. Slowly but determinedly, he wrote his name, “Thank you,” and then the date. This was the result of an 11-month-long rehabilitation enabled by an implant in his brain. Before that process, Dong could move his arms slightly but wasn’t able to use his fingers. “I couldn’t believe I was able to write again. I was so excited I even missed a stroke in my name,” he told MIT Technology Review on a video call.  In November 2024, Dong became one of the first people in China to be given an invasive brain-computer interface (BCI) through brain surgery. He had signed up for a clinical trial with the device’s developer one month after seeing on TV how a BCI had apparently enabled another paralyzed Chinese man to hold his granddaughter.  This March, the implant Dong uses became the first invasive BCI product in the world to be approved for use beyond clinical trials. It’s now available to some patients with paralysis in their limbs due to spinal cord injuries. We spoke to a range of experts to understand why the device was able to reach this global milestone, what makes this moment so significant, and what to expect next.  A world first Dong’s brain implant is a coin-size device called NEO. It was developed by Neuracle Technology , a Shanghai-based startup, together with researchers at Tsinghua University in Beijing.  During a procedure that took just over an hour and a half, the device’s sensors, which collect Dong’s brain signals, were placed on his dura mater, the tough outer layer of tissue that covers and protects the brain. The signals are transmitted to a computer by an implant placed on Dong’s skull. The computer then translates the signals into commands for a soft robotic glove Dong
